title: What is a time series?
subtitle: Start with one measurement. No PromQL or SQL knowledge needed.

lessons.title: A number needs a meaning
lessons.definition: A metric describes something we measure. A sample records its value at a particular time.
lessons.analogy: A café writes “4 people waiting at 10:00”. The number, unit, and time answer different questions.
lessons.body:
The metric queue_depth tells us what is being measured: people waiting. Its value, 4, tells us how many. The timestamp tells us when the measurement was taken. Without the unit, 4 could mean people, seconds, or bytes. Without the timestamp, we cannot tell whether the measurement is current.

A sample is one observation of a series. Begin by reading it aloud: “At this time, this thing had this value.” Prometheus collects measurements at intervals called scrapes; it does not normally record every individual request as a separate event.
lessons.sql_connection: Think of one SQL row with timestamp and value columns. The column name and schema explain the unit. You do not need SQL to understand the observation: when, what, and how much.

lessons.title: Samples become a time series
lessons.definition: A time series is a sequence of samples for the same measurement identity over time.
lessons.analogy: Take a photo of the same café queue every 30 seconds. The sequence tells the story that one photo cannot.
lessons.body:
Suppose the queue has 2 people at 10:00, 4 at 10:00:30, and 6 at 10:01. These are three samples of one series. Joining the points on a chart helps us see change, but the stored measurements are the points, not a continuous movie.

A scrape is a collection attempt. Events may happen between scrapes, and a failed scrape can leave a gap. More samples mean more history for the same series; they do not automatically mean more distinct series.
lessons.sql_connection: Three SQL rows with the same metric and labels but different timestamps represent three samples of one series. ORDER BY timestamp puts them in time order; it does not combine their values.

check.explanation: More timestamps add history to a series. They do not change its identity.
check.concept: The same queue is measured at three times. How many series is that?

lessons.title: Labels tell similar measurements apart
lessons.definition: A series is identified by its metric name and its complete set of labels.
lessons.analogy: Two cafés can both have a queue of 4 people. A location label tells us whose queue each value describes.
lessons.body:
An instance is one running copy of an application. queue_depth{instance="a"} and queue_depth{instance="b"} are different series, even when their values happen to match. A service label can say which application the instance belongs to. A label is descriptive text; it is not another measured value.

Changing any label changes the series identity. Changing only the value or timestamp adds another sample to the existing series. In our first lab, the metric name app_active_sessions is a complete beginner query: it asks for the available active-session series at one evaluation time.
lessons.sql_connection: Labels resemble identifying columns such as service and instance. Several rows can belong to one series when those identifying columns match. Filtering a metric name is similar to selecting rows for that measurement.

title: Counters and gauges
subtitle: Learn “how many so far?” versus “how many right now?”

lessons.title: Counter: how many so far?
lessons.definition: A counter accumulates events. It rises as events occur and may reset when the process restarts.
lessons.analogy: A café receipt counter shows how many orders have been served since the till started.
lessons.body:
If the request counter reads 100 and later reads 110, ten more requests were counted. The value 110 is a running total; it does not say “110 requests per second”. A quiet period leaves the counter unchanged. Ending a request does not subtract from a requests-served counter.

Counters are useful for events such as requests, errors, or completed jobs. Names often end in _total, but a name is a convention, not proof of correct instrumentation. Later we will turn changes in this total into a speed using rate().
lessons.sql_connection: A counter sample is like a periodically saved running total. SUM of those snapshots counts earlier events repeatedly. Counting raw event rows is a different data model from sampling a cumulative counter.

steps.explanation: This is the total already accumulated when we begin watching.

steps.explanation: Another 10 requests make the total 120. New events add to the old total.

steps.explanation: More events cause a bigger jump. The graph still stores totals, not speed.

steps.explanation: The current total answers “how many so far?”. To ask “how fast?”, compare samples over elapsed time.

lessons.remember: A counter value is a cumulative total, not a per-second rate.

options: 110 events happened in the latest second
check.explanation: A counter value is a cumulative total, not a per-second rate.
check.concept: A counter rises from 100 to 110 without a reset. What happened?

lessons.title: Gauge: how much right now?
lessons.definition: A gauge measures a current amount that can naturally increase or decrease.
lessons.analogy: The number of people currently waiting rises when someone joins and falls when someone is served.
lessons.body:
A queue of 2 people can become 4 and then 1. The drop from 4 to 1 is ordinary behavior, not a restart. Temperature, free memory, active sessions, and queue depth are examples of gauges. Some gauges can be negative when that makes sense for their unit.

Choose a gauge for a current state or balance. Choose a counter for accumulating events. For a gauge, its current value, recent average, minimum, or maximum are often useful. Applying counter rate logic to an ordinary falling gauge can produce a misleading result.
lessons.sql_connection: A gauge resembles a balance recorded at different times. Selecting the latest row reads the current balance; averaging a time window summarizes recorded balances. Treating every decrease as a reset would corrupt that meaning.

lessons.title: A restart is different from a falling gauge
lessons.definition: A counter reset starts a new accumulation period; a falling gauge describes a smaller current amount.
lessons.analogy: Restarting the café till clears its receipt counter. Serving a waiting customer only shortens the queue.
lessons.body:
Imagine counter samples 100, 115, 5, 20, 35. A reset happened between the second and third samples. Subtracting the first value from the last gives a negative answer, which cannot describe a negative number of requests. Prometheus counter functions detect decreases and adjust for resets.

The adjustment cannot recover events that were never observed before a restart. It is an estimate from available samples. Metric type is therefore a promise about what a measurement means, not just how its line looks. A gauge can happen to rise for a while without becoming a counter.
lessons.sql_connection: A SQL implementation would need explicit reset-aware delta logic, typically using LAG to inspect the previous counter sample. A simple last-minus-first calculation cannot distinguish a restart from a genuine balance decrease.

title: Histograms, one observation at a time
subtitle: Understand durations, buckets, and cumulative counts before learning percentiles.

lessons.title: Why one average is not the whole story
lessons.definition: A histogram summarizes the distribution of many observations, such as request durations.
lessons.analogy: Two cafés can have the same average waiting time, while one occasionally makes a customer wait much longer.
lessons.body:
An observation is one event’s measured value: for example, one request took 0.42 seconds. A histogram does not normally store every original duration for later inspection. It counts observations into groups called buckets and also keeps a total count and sum.

This lets us ask how much of the traffic was fast or slow. The average uses the sum and count, but loses information about the shape and tail of the distribution. Begin with four durations and watch what is retained as they enter a histogram.
lessons.sql_connection: If SQL has raw duration rows, you can inspect every request and calculate exact sample statistics. Prometheus classic histogram buckets retain counts at boundaries instead; the original duration rows cannot be reconstructed from those counts.

lessons.title: A bucket is a counting rule
lessons.definition: A histogram bucket counts observations that satisfy a boundary condition.
lessons.analogy: Imagine a sign saying “count every customer served within 0.5 seconds”. The sign defines a bucket.
lessons.body:
For a bucket with upper bound 0.5 seconds, a duration of 0.42 qualifies and a duration of 0.8 does not. The boundary is inclusive: 0.5 itself qualifies. The boundary is a duration; the bucket value is a count. Confusing those two units is a common source of errors.

A conventional histogram chart often draws separate intervals. Prometheus classic buckets instead use cumulative upper bounds. We will make that difference explicit in the next lesson. For now, follow one observation and decide which upper-bound rules it satisfies.
lessons.sql_connection: A bucket count is like COUNT(*) WHERE duration <= 0.5. The SQL predicate describes the bucket’s inclusive boundary. It is not SELECT duration, and the bucket value is not a latency measurement.

check.prompt: What does a bucket value of 20 mean?
check.explanation: A bucket boundary is a measured-value limit; its stored value is a count.

lessons.title: Prometheus buckets are cumulative
lessons.definition: A classic bucket with label le="x" counts every observation less than or equal to x.
lessons.analogy: A short person qualifies under several height limits. A fast request likewise contributes to several duration buckets.
lessons.body:
The label le means “less than or equal”. A 0.42-second observation increments the 0.5-second, 1-second, and +Inf buckets. It does not increment the 0.1-second bucket. Larger buckets include the counts already present in smaller buckets, so adding all bucket values would double-count observations.

The +Inf bucket has no finite upper limit and includes every observation. Subtract neighboring cumulative buckets to find an interval count: count(0.5 < duration <= 1) equals bucket(le=1) minus bucket(le=0.5). Cumulative means both inclusion across bounds and accumulation over events.
lessons.sql_connection: Several COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE duration <= bound) expressions reproduce cumulative buckets from raw rows. Subtract neighboring cumulative counts for a disjoint interval. Do not SUM all cumulative bucket columns to count requests.

lessons.title: Read _bucket, _count, and _sum
lessons.definition: A classic histogram exposes bucket counters, an observation counter, and a sum of observed values.
lessons.analogy: A café ledger can retain how many orders there were, total time spent serving them, and counts below each service-time limit.
lessons.body:
The _count series counts observations; it equals the +Inf bucket. The _sum series adds their measured values. For nonnegative request durations, both behave like counters. With four durations 0.12, 0.42, 0.8, and 1.4 seconds, the count is 4 and the sum is 2.74 seconds. Their ratio is 0.685 seconds per request.

That is the mean of the accumulated observations, not a p95. Later, rate(_sum)/rate(_count) will describe a recent mean rather than a lifetime mean. Observations that can be negative need extra care because their sum may decrease.
lessons.sql_connection: Raw SQL duration rows support COUNT(*) and SUM(duration), whose ratio gives the mean. The matching Prometheus suffixes describe stored totals, not SQL operators that are automatically run at query time.

title: Read your first PromQL expressions
subtitle: Select the right series, then choose the time you want to examine.

lessons.title: One moment versus a window
lessons.definition: An instant vector has one value per selected series at an evaluation time; a range vector contains samples over a window.
lessons.analogy: An instant view is a photo of several queues now. A range vector is a short photo album for each queue.
lessons.body:
The word vector here means a collection. queue_depth selects series at one evaluation time. queue_depth[5m] supplies recent samples separately for each series, normally as input to a function. The stored metric type (counter or gauge) is different from the query’s result type (scalar, instant vector, or range vector).

A range query is another idea: it evaluates an expression repeatedly at multiple times to draw a chart. A range vector is an expression’s time-window input. Real instant selectors also use lookback and staleness rules, so “latest usable sample” need not mean a sample with exactly the evaluation timestamp.
lessons.sql_connection: A snapshot table resembles one instant view. Timestamp-filtered history resembles a range-vector input. A chart runs calculations at many times; that is different from merely returning one set of historical rows.

lessons.title: Filter labels before doing arithmetic
lessons.definition: Label matchers select the series whose descriptive labels satisfy your conditions.
lessons.analogy: Before comparing queues, choose the café location and the till you actually want to study.
lessons.body:
up{service="api"} selects the availability series whose service label equals api. Commas inside braces mean AND. The matchers = and != compare exact label strings; =~ and !~ use regular expressions. Prometheus label regexes are fully anchored, so =~"api" matches the entire value api rather than api-server.

A matcher that accepts an empty string can also match a missing label. This is not automatically the same as SQL NULL behavior. Filtering changes which series are considered; it does not change their measured values.
lessons.sql_connection: Exact matchers resemble WHERE service = 'api'. Multiple predicates combine with AND. For equivalent regex behavior in this DuckDB lab, REGEXP_FULL_MATCH is closer than a substring search. Missing-label and NULL semantics still differ.

title: From totals to speed
subtitle: Build rate(), irate(), and increase() from visible counter changes.

lessons.title: Change divided by time is a speed
lessons.definition: A per-second rate measures how quickly a counter increases, not how large its total is.
lessons.analogy: An odometer tells distance traveled. Speed compares the change in distance with the time it took.
lessons.body:
If a counter rises by 30 requests over 15 seconds, the observed interval speed is 30 / 15 = 2 requests per second. Dividing by the number of samples would use the wrong denominator: samples are observations, not seconds. A larger historical counter can still be growing more slowly than a smaller one.

PromQL rate(counter[window]) estimates a per-second increase using the selected samples, reset handling, and boundary extrapolation. The animation begins with the simple change-over-time idea. The later lessons explain why the real function is more careful than subtracting two arbitrary values.
lessons.sql_connection: LAG(value) and timestamp differences can calculate observed adjacent deltas in SQL. This is an intuition for rate, not a full implementation of Prometheus reset handling and extrapolation.

lessons.definition: rate() estimates average increase across a window; irate() uses only the latest two samples in that window.
lessons.analogy: Average trip speed and the speed between your last two roadside markers can disagree during a sudden acceleration.

Use the same counter samples: 100, 110, 120, 130, 190 at 15-second intervals. The last interval adds 60 requests in 15 seconds: irate is 4 requests/second. lessons.definition: Counter functions adjust observed decreases so a restart is not mistaken for negative event traffic.
lessons.analogy: Add up the receipts from before and after the till restart, rather than subtracting the new till display from the old one.

For samples 100, 115, 5, 20, 35, the observed reset-adjusted changes are 15, 5, 15, and 15: a total of 50. The unknown activity between the last old-process scrape and the restart cannot be reconstructed perfectly. Counter functions work from available observations.

lessons.title: increase() answers “how many during this window?”
lessons.definition: increase() estimates the counter increase over the full selected window, while rate() expresses it per second.
lessons.analogy: “Two orders per second” is a speed. “About 120 orders in a minute” is a quantity over an interval.
lessons.body:
For counters, increase(x[window]) is rate(x[window]) multiplied by the window duration in seconds. Prometheus extrapolates toward the window boundaries when samples do not land exactly on them, subject to its extrapolation rules. Therefore the result may be fractional even when the underlying events are whole requests.

In the 75-second animation example, rate is 1.5 requests/second and increase is 112.5 requests. The observed first-to-last change is only 90 across 60 seconds; the additional amount is a boundary estimate, not an extra stored sample. This distinction is why “last minus first” is not always exact increase().
lessons.sql_connection: SQL SUM of reset-aware adjacent deltas estimates observed change. Matching increase exactly also requires Prometheus extrapolation and its treatment of boundary gaps. Multiplying an accurate per-second rate by a duration changes the unit to events.

title: Calculate over time
subtitle: Understand sum_over_time, avg_over_time, and the question each function answers.

lessons.title: sum_over_time() adds samples, not new events
lessons.definition: sum_over_time() adds the sampled values inside each series’s selected time window.
lessons.analogy: If three queue photos show 2, 4, and 6 people, adding the photo counts gives 12—not necessarily 12 different people.
lessons.body:
sum_over_time(queue_depth[90s]) computes one sum per queue series. In our teaching example, the selected values 2, 4, 6 sum to 12. This is a sum of snapshots: the same waiting person could appear in multiple photos. It is not automatically a count of arrivals, nor a time integral.

More frequent scrapes can increase the sum even when the real-world situation is unchanged. Adding samples of a cumulative counter is especially misleading for event counts because earlier events are repeated in later totals. Use increase on a counter when you want interval event counts.
lessons.sql_connection: For one series, this is SUM(value) over timestamp-filtered rows. It adds measured snapshots. To count raw events in SQL you would need event rows, a different table from sampled metric values.

title: Combine series without losing meaning
subtitle: Separate aggregation across series from calculation across time.

lessons.title: sum() and sum_over_time() use different axes
lessons.definition: sum() combines series at one evaluation time; sum_over_time() combines samples within each series.
lessons.analogy: Adding today’s queues across cafés differs from adding one café’s queue photos across the morning.
lessons.body:
Suppose instance a has recent values 2,4,6 and b has 1,3,5. At the final time, sum(queue_depth) is 6+5=11 across instances. Over the illustrated window, sum_over_time gives 12 for a and 9 for b. It keeps their histories separate.

You can intentionally combine the two operations, but first say which axis each one reduces: labels/series, or time. count(metric) counts series at an instant; count_over_time(metric[window]) counts samples separately within each series. Neither automatically counts counter events.

lessons.definition: Vector arithmetic pairs series using a matching key made from their labels.

When dividing two instant vectors, Prometheus does not combine rows by their visual position on the screen. It matches their label sets according to the operator’s matching rules. subtitle: Estimate p95 only after you understand what the buckets retain.

lessons.title: What p95 actually means
lessons.definition: The 95th percentile is a value at or below which roughly 95% of the observation population lies.
lessons.analogy: Line up 100 customer wait times from shortest to longest and find the boundary around the 95th position.
lessons.body:
Classic histograms retain bucket counts rather than raw durations. histogram_quantile estimates a percentile inside the bucket containing the desired rank. With cumulative counts 20,60,90,100 at bounds 0.1,0.5,1,2 seconds, the 95th observation lies in the 1-to-2-second bucket. Linear interpolation estimates 1.5 seconds.

That interpolation assumes a distribution inside the bucket; it does not reveal the exact original 95th duration. Wide buckets limit precision. A tail percentile describes a population, not a promise that every request will finish within that time.
lessons.sql_connection: PERCENTILE_CONT over raw duration rows uses information the bucketed histogram no longer retains. Computing a percentile over bucket counts themselves is a different, meaningless latency calculation.

When comparing current and past values, match the populations, windows, and labels. Our fixed demonstration data covers limited historical windows, so an offset pointing into a gap may correctly produce no data. An absent historical result is not automatically a zero baseline.

lessons.title: Subqueries and recording rules reuse calculations
lessons.definition: A subquery samples an expression over time; a recording rule saves an expression’s results periodically.
lessons.analogy: You can repeatedly calculate a service total for an album, or keep writing that total into a reusable log.
lessons.body:
A subquery such as (sum(queue_depth))[5m:30s] evaluates the inner expression on a repeated time grid, producing a range of calculated results. The 30s part is the subquery resolution, not the scrape interval. An outer function can summarize those calculated samples.

A recording rule periodically stores the result of a useful expression as a new series. It can reduce repeated query work, but its rule interval and labels affect interpretation. Deep or broad subqueries can be expensive; inspect the data volume and prefer clear, reusable calculations.

lessons.title: An alert window is not an alert hold timer
lessons.definition: An expression chooses evidence; an alert’s for duration controls how long a condition must remain active before firing.
lessons.analogy: A café might inspect the last five minutes of service, but call for help only after a problem persists for another two minutes.
lessons.body:
A rate(...[5m]) expression looks backward over five minutes at each evaluation. An alert rule with for: 2m waits for its condition to remain active across rule evaluations before firing. These two durations have different jobs. Pending means the condition is active but the hold duration has not yet been satisfied.

If the condition stops being active during the pending period, the hold timer normally resets. Missing data may remove a vector element entirely; handle absence deliberately rather than assuming it behaves like a numeric zero. A useful alert should identify an actionable symptom and the affected service.

Adding labels multiplies the possible combinations that become separate series. Bounded labels such as service or status can be useful; unbounded request_id or user_id labels can create expensive, rapidly growing populations. Longer histories and wider query windows add more samples to process.

title: Explain an incident with evidence
subtitle: Combine the fundamentals into a careful reliability investigation.

lessons.title: Read traffic, errors, latency, and availability together
lessons.definition: An incident explanation uses several compatible signals rather than one alarming number.
lessons.analogy: A long café queue might reflect a rush of customers, slower service, a broken till, or several causes together.
lessons.body:
Start by checking the population and time window. Throughput comes from request-counter rates; error fraction compares aligned error and total rates; latency comes from the request-duration distribution; up describes scrape availability. These signals answer related but different questions.

A rising error count can simply accompany more traffic, while an error fraction reveals how large the affected share is. A latency percentile can change even when the average stays similar. None of these alone proves a root cause. Compare normal and incident scenarios, form a hypothesis, and look for evidence that could disprove it.
lessons.sql_connection: A careful SQL investigation similarly aligns populations and time windows before joining derived statistics. Correlation between grouped results is evidence to investigate, not proof of a causal explanation.

lessons.title: An SLO defines the reliability goal
lessons.definition: A service-level objective states the desired share of good events over a specified period.
lessons.analogy: A café promises that at least 999 of every 1,000 orders meet its success criterion over the agreed reporting period.
lessons.body:
A 99.9% success SLO allows a bad-event fraction of 0.1%, or 0.001. Define good and bad events precisely, including which requests belong in the denominator. An availability or latency objective can use a different definition of good, so do not mix them without explanation.

A monthly objective is evaluated over its reporting period. A short five-minute error spike can threaten the budget, but does not by itself establish that the monthly SLO has already been violated. Window, population, and units remain as important here as in the very first metric lesson.
lessons.sql_connection: An SLO calculation is a carefully defined numerator divided by a denominator over an agreed interval. Filtering the two populations differently can produce a mathematically valid ratio that answers the wrong business question.

lessons.title: Burn rate turns an error fraction into budget pressure
lessons.definition: Burn rate is the observed bad-event fraction divided by the allowed bad-event fraction.
lessons.analogy: It asks how fast you are spending the allowed failure budget compared with the sustainable pace.
lessons.body:
With a 99.9% success objective, the allowed bad fraction is 0.001. An observed error fraction of 0.01 is therefore a burn rate of 10. It indicates ten times the sustainable fraction for that observation window, assuming the objective definition is aligned. It is not automatically ten minutes remaining.

A useful response compares short and longer windows, checks traffic volume and missing data, and investigates associated latency and availability. Finish the capstone by writing the requested threshold query, then explain its population, time window, unit, and limitations in plain language.
lessons.sql_connection: The same ratio can be computed from aligned SQL good/bad event counts. Calculating time remaining in a budget needs additional period and traffic assumptions; it does not follow from the burn-rate number alone.

SELECT service,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = '500' THEN value ELSE 0 END)
    / NULLIF(SUM(value), 0) AS cumulative_error_fraction
FROM snapshot WHERE metric = 'http_requests_total'
GROUP BY service
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN status = '500' THEN value ELSE 0 END)
    / NULLIF(SUM(value), 0) > 0.05;
equivalence: The SQL illustrates grouped threshold filtering on accumulated counts. The PromQL condition uses recent rates and can differ after resets or changing traffic.
